#4697. Janus Electric secures battery supply deal for its battery-swap semi truck

Australian conversion specialists Janus Electric have been celebrating a growing slate of orders for their Class 8 electric truck conversions, which ditch diesel in favor of advanced battery-swap electric power – but exactly how they’d deliver all those trucks was still a question. Now, we have an answer: Electrovaya will supply the batteries.

The concept of dropping an electric power unit into a Class 8 semi makes perfect sense, as most of these trucks are built as gliders. That is, rolling body and chassis without an engine and transmission that’s ready to receive power from Cummins, Detroit, International, or Volvo Penta. That’s the role that Janus Electric sees itself occupying, and it seems to be working.

Janus’ reservation book crept past 70 units this past summer, helped along in part by California’s HVIP Program and the US EPA’s Diesel Emission Reduction Act (DERA) Grants. When the HVIP voucher is combined with the Port of Los Angeles’ “Plus” support, customers can received up to $166,000 per truck conversion. Factor in the massive fuel savings of electric and the classic good looks of square-nose Western Star truck body, and it’s easy to see why they’d be a popular choice.

As Jerry Seinfeld taught us however, it’s one thing to take a reservation – it’s another thing to deliver. To help make it happen, Janus has inked a battery supply deal with Electrovaya that will see a $26 million initial purchase orders for Electrovaya battery packs to demand for Janus’ products in the US and Canada, along with the battery company purchasing approximately $1.4 million in Janus stock with (what seems to be) actual money.

“Electrovaya is an important partner to Janus Electric, and we’re particularly pleased it has decided to invest directly in our business,” explains Ben Hutt, Managing Director and CEO of Janus Electric. “The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport.”

The Janus Electric-repowered trucks carry a stout, 480 hp electric motor drawing power from a standard 310 kWh battery pack, with up to two battery packs (one on each side) of the truck. In practice, that gives the Janus trucks up to 370 miles of loaded range. After that, the batteries can be DC fast charged in under 90 minutes, or swapped for fresh ones in about four minutes without too much in the way of specialized equipment. That’s not just Janus’ killer app, it means that a battery supply deal like this one with a strategic partner who’s invested in the fledgling company’s success is such a huge deal.

“Reliable battery supply is critical to our growth,” adds Hutt, “and Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale. Both companies see considerable opportunity in this market, and we look forward to building on our partnership.”

For their part, Electrovoya executives seem to know their role here, and seem excited to be a part of what Janus is doing. “Class 8 trucking is one of the most exciting and demanding frontiers in electrification, and Janus has demonstrated real commercial traction with fleets in the US, Canada and Australia,” said Dr. Raj Das Gupta, CEO of Electrovaya. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations.”

Electrovaya will be expanding its American manufacturing capacity with lithium-ion cell, module, and battery pack production at its new, potentially BABA-compliant facility in Jamestown, New York, which is expected to come online in 2027.

You’ll hear lots of people blathering on about deep fried turkey this year, but smoking the bird is a secret hack to making things way more delicious. Amazon has Weber’s Smoque pellet smokers at their lowest prices of 2026, so you can grab one now and perfect your technique before guests show up for turkey day. The discounts in Weber’s Amazon storefront cover its pellet smokers and Slate tabletop griddles along with the tongs and spatulas that hang off the side of a grill. As an added bonus, a smoker won’t burn your house down like a turkey fryer might.

A set-it-and-walk-away smoker for holiday turkey and brisket

Pellet smokers make it easy to cook low and slow. An electric auger pushes a carefully measured amount of wood pellets into a burn pot to keep your temp in the perfect zone. The Weber Smoque 22-inch pellet smoker is down to $599, its lowest price of 2026. Weber rates it for temperatures up to 500°F and says its SmokeBoost setting is tuned for deeper smoke flavor. The Rapid React PID controller, per Weber, heats up fast and recovers temperature after you open the lid, which matters when you’re spritzing ribs every hour. Two food probes come in the box and plug into built-in ports, so you can track two cuts at once. If you want to sear as well as smoke, the Weber Searwood 600 goes up to 600°F and is $899. A propane flat-top small enough for the patio table

Long enough to flip sausages without singeing your knuckles

#4695. We Found the Best Adjustable Dumbbells for Every Home Gym

Looking to make more gains while taking up less space? These picks from SMRTFT, PowerBlock, and REP Fitness pack a big punch in a small package.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF THERE'S ONE piece of home gym equipment anyone can make room for at home, it's a pair of adjustable dumbbells. These clever pieces of fitness gear require minimal space, shifting from light to heavy with a quick turn of a knob or tweak of a setting. They simplify things by tackling two challenges of working out at home: space and equipment. Think about it: A single pair of adjustable dumbbells can replace around 15 standard dumbbells.

"There's a reason dumbbells are in every single big-box gym," says MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., who created an arm-focused muscle-building program, All Out Arms, based heavily around dumbbells. "If you want targeted muscle—and that’s what all guys want—then you want dumbbells." Adjustable dumbbells (just like adjustable kettlebells) offer a range of weights from one compact footprint, eliminating the need for multiple sets of weights.

If you prefer working out at home (or do so out of necessity on days when you can't make it to the gym), a pair of adjustable dumbbells is a solution that helps you stay consistent with your training without leaving your home. These are effective pieces, especially when combined with cardio equipment and a great weight bench. Check out our top picks for the best adjustable dumbbells for your home gym right now.

"The Nüobell is the best blend of reliability and authentic dumbbell feel I’ve used," says Samuel, who has been using these for over three years. "The shape and design of these 'bells make them ideal for accessory motions, like skullcrushers and biceps curls, and they’re easy to hold for goblet squats too." Aside from a few scratches, they've held up great to three years of heavy use.

With a maximum weight of 80 pounds of weight per dumbbell and a feel that's nearly indistinguishable from traditional dumbbells, users can utilize the same set of weights for a complete full-body workout. Users can quickly drop down to lower weights for exercises like bent-over flies or pile on the plates for more intense squats. "It features a 'turn-and-click' design rather than just a built-in selector," notes Williams. Users simply turn the handle until they reach their desired weight.

During testing, Howell noted that the Nüobell arrived assembled and was easy to plug-and-play once unboxed. Of all the adjustable dumbbells he tried, these felt the most like actual dumbbells. "These feel like the next evolution of the traditional dumbbells we have become used to in gyms," Howell said.

The major defining features include: metal plates and handles, top-tier construction, easy click-and-go weight adjustment, and the selected weight displayed on the dumbbell itself.

However, Howell expressed some concerns about the rack it came with, feeling it might have been an afterthought. He questioned whether the tempered plastic rack would withstand the constant re-racking of the metal plates over time. Nevertheless, he emphasized that the actual dumbbells are well-crafted and feel solid as hell.

In Howell's opinion, these dumbbells are best for someone who has invested in a home gym and is serious about fitness. They are tailored for the hardcore client who likely has a squat rack and barbell in their garage as well, but wants to add an elite set of adjustable dumbbells to their training arsenal. If you’re building the mother of all home gyms and money is no object, this comprehensive premium set of dumbbells from SMRTFT might just be your best pick.

These BowFlex adjustable dumbbells adjust from 5 to 52.5 pounds in 2.5-pound increments, which replaces up to 15 pairs of dumbbells (that’s a lot of potential time and money saved). We love that the weight distribution is close to that of traditional dumbbells, and the 2.5-pound increments offer more customization in weight ranges. No matter how these BowFlex dumbbells are ordered, they arrive at your door in two separate, well-packed boxes.

The weight is adjusted through selection dials located on either side of each dumbbell. The dial system is easy to use, though not exactly as streamlined as SMRTFT's single-twist mechanism. Keep in mind that changing the weight requires docking and adjusting both sides of each dumbbell–that’s two dial adjustments for each change in weight. But I prefer them to PowerBlock dumbbells.

The previous version of the SelectTechs had a plastic casing, but these updated models now feature premium metal components that are better protected from damage. We find the design a bit wide and cumbersome for certain exercises, such as triceps extensions. "In my experience, these work best for chest-supported rows and overhead presses," says Samuel.

These dumbbells have been in regular use in my garage for half a year, I haven't had any issues with wear or tear. That said, it's essential to handle them with care and consider your exercise preferences when incorporating them into your home gym setup. Like most of the dumbbells on this list, it's probably not a great idea to drop these on the floor after finishing a set.

The last note is that advanced lifters may feel a little constrained by the 52.5-pound max weight and may want to consider the 90-pound-max-weight BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 1090s instead.

Read More: Our Review of the BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 552 Dumbbells

The NordicTrack Select-A-Weight Dumbbells are sturdy and easy to use, featuring metal plates and a robust plastic casing designed to withstand the occasional drop (though we don't recommend it). With a weight range of 10 to 55 pounds per dumbbell, adjustable in 2.5-pound increments, they cater especially well to home workouts. However, they're not our top pick for accessory movements due to their relatively broad plates.

This set arrived assembled and was ready to go once unboxed. "I appreciated that it came with a tray that gave it a home and an easy-to-store footprint," noted Howell. "Making changes in weight by 2.5-pound increments was fairly easy, and they felt really sturdy and safe even when adjusted to heavier loads—the knurled metal handle helped with this."What Howell didn't love about these was that there was no way to confirm what weight you were using once the 'bells' were removed from the rack. Only the rack is labeled with weight numbers, not the actual dumbbell."I think this is an ideal product for someone who knows their way around a gym and is looking for a solid addition to their home to supplement," says Howell. "They're perfect for an intermediate client."

In terms of sound, while "these are quieter than other adjustable dumbbells on the market, they make more noise than the PowerBlocks," explains Samuel. Additionally, if you wish to incorporate barbell movements into your home workout routine, we've found that these dumbbells work seamlessly with the Hyperbell.

One of my favorite equipment makers, I was surprised how long it took REP Fitness to come out with a viable adjustable dumbbell option. But it seems like they were waiting to create something special, and that's what they've done with the QuickDraws.

The plates can be adjusted in 2.5-pound increments, spanning from 5 to 30 pounds. For those heavy lifters, 30 pounds might not be enough, but for the average user looking for a quick pump in the arms or lighter weights for perfect accessory movements, this is a great pick. For anyone who wants to increase the weight, REP Fitness offers heavier options with the same streamlined design, for up to 60 pounds.

They've patented their Lock-N-Load adjustment system, which is straightforward and lets you change the weights by flipping a switch on each dumbbell. This system allows you to swap weights quickly, so you can change the load between dumbbell exercises and avoid stalling.

For our testing, the dumbbells arrived in two boxes and require minimal assembly, making them an ultra-accessible choice for delivery and home use.

PowerBlock adjustable dumbbells are an ultra-sturdy set designed for lasting performance, perfect for executing heavy-duty moves like dead stop rows, Romanian deadlifts, and heavy presses. At just 12 inches long with the storage stand, these dumbbells offer decent compactness and versatility.

The Pro 50 Adjustable Dumbbells cover a weight range of 5 to 50 pounds per dumbbell, with adjustments in increments of 2.5 pounds. This weight range suits beginners well, and more experienced lifters can expand the weight by opting for additional expansion kits. For those who find 50 pounds per dumbbell insufficient, PowerBlock offers heavier models such as the Elite USA (up to 90 pounds per dumbbell) or the Pro 100 EXP (up to 100 pounds per dumbbell). Most models of adjustable dumbbells by PowerBlock feature the same pin-and-lock adjustment mechanism, which is easy to use and avoids jamming issues found in some other systems.

In his testing, Howell pointed out the compact structure of the actual dumbbell, noting the plate-like weights, which are more like weighted frames than traditional circular ones. Howell found this design "genius", as the square nature of the dumbbell makes it easy to lay down once done using it without it rolling away or requiring a rack to rest it in. He also appreciated that they arrived assembled and were fairly easy to unpack and begin using.

However, Howell expressed concerns about the durability of certain components, such as the handles and the "clip" that allows you to lock your chosen weight in, which are made of plastic. He believes these dumbbells might not be robust enough for consistent use, particularly for hardcore gymgoers.

Despite these concerns, Samuel praises their adjustability and durability, stating, "I've never encountered a more durable adjustable dumbbell. I love them for farmer’s walks, heavy DB lunges, and thrusters, and rely on them anytime I do a metcon-style workout at home." Samuel also shared he’s dropped these from three or four feet up after tough sets of incline presses, "and they hold up just fine." (Although it's not advisable to make a habit of dropping any adjustable dumbbells regularly.)These dumbbells feature comfortable contoured handles that enhance grip during workouts. However, they do not provide the same weight distribution as traditional dumbbells, as Samuel points out: "If you’re looking to use a set of adjustable movements for plenty of accessory movements, go with something more dumbbell-shaped."

Look for a weight range that meets your fitness goals. Most adjustable dumbbells can be adjusted in 2.5- or 5-pound increments, so it's important to consider a weight range that fits your needs.

Adjustable dumbbells come in different shapes and sizes. Consider the size and shape of the dumbbells and make sure they feel comfortable in your hands. Basically, does the dumbbell feel "good" or natural to you? Again, this comes down to personal preference and might involve some trial and error.

Some adjustable dumbbells distribute the load differently than traditional dumbbells (atypical), changing how it responds to certain movements (particularly accessory movements). A good rule of thumb is if you're looking to perform heavier exercises (farmer's carries, RDLs, rows) you can consider an adjustable dumbbell that doesn't distribute its weight like a traditional dumbbell, such as the PowerBlock option featured above. If you're planning to do more accessory movements (like biceps curls or skull crushers), opt for a traditional dumbbell-shaped option.

There are a few different mechanisms adjustable dumbbells use to switch weights, with some being easier or more user-friendly.

This mechanism uses a dial on the end of the dumbbell handle to adjust the weight. To change the weight, you turn the dial to the desired weight, and the mechanism will lock in the appropriate weight plates. Some adjustable dumbbells must be docked in their storage base to change weight using a dial, while others can be adjusted outside their docking station.

This mechanism uses a pin to select the desired weight and can take some practice to get used to if you're new to it. To change the weight, pull out the pin, select the desired weight, then reinsert the pin into the corresponding slot to lock it in.

This mechanism uses a twist-locking mechanism to secure the weight plates. To change the weight, you twist the handle to unlock the weight plates, remove or add weight plates, and then twist the handle back to lock in the new weight.

Warranties reflect a manufacturer's confidence in its product. And with some of the best adjustable dumbbells priced at or above $500, you want to be sure your investment is protected. So, it’s important to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous five-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest training equipment, including adjustable dumbbells. To build this guide, I tested more than 30 adjustable dumbbells over the past five years, drawing on my experience and that of my fellow MH fitness editors, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. Samuel utilized the top-performing adjustable dumbbells featured in this guide in fitness programs with several of his advanced clients.

We also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn, to test and assess how well these dumbbells performed in the real world (read: a high-traffic training facility). In addition, we sought insights from trainers from both our MH Advisory Board and our Strength in Diversity class for further anecdotal and experiential perspectives on the top adjustable dumbbells.

Each dumbbell was rigorously tested in a variety of categories, including durability, weight distribution, ease of shifting between weights, and aesthetics. All dumbbells were tested with three types of exercises: explosive exercises (such as cleans), multi-joint strength exercises (such as bench presses and Romanian deadlifts), and accessory movements (such as biceps curls and lateral raises). All dumbbells were also dropped from a standard bench to test baseline durability (no adjustable dumbbell should ever be dropped from shoulder height), and they were monitored for signs of rust over a three-month period.

Adjustable dumbbells pack a ton of perks compared to regular dumbbells, with the most obvious being their space-saving design: No matter which adjustable dumbbells you choose, you can guarantee they'll take up less space than the sets of traditional dumbbells they replace.

Another attractive benefit of adjustable dumbbells is that they're more cost-effective than multiple sets of traditional dumbbells. A lot of the options on this list aren't exactly budget buys, we know. But building out a weight rack with 5-15 sets of high-quality traditional dumbbells can add up in cost even quicker.

This comes down to three things: space, personal preference, and how you plan to use your dumbbells. If you have unlimited space, you can definitely consider standard dumbbells.

"If you're building out a home gym and especially if you like to train accessory motions and work through a full range of motion, you still can't beat standard dumbbells," explains Samuel.

"They're going to be more durable, have better weight distribution for most moves, and, as cool as some adjustment dial might be, there's nothing more efficient than literally putting a 35-pound dumbbell down and picking a 40-pounder up."

But if you're in tight confines or like to work out on the go, opt for a good adjustable option. "You can load a pair of Powerblocks in your trunk much more easily than you can load 10 pairs of dumbbells for a road trip."

You'll also want to consider how often you'll drop your dumbbells. Even the best, most durable adjustable dumbbells on this list still have weight-switching mechanisms and won't hold up to being routinely dropped from a few feet in the air after a set of shoulder presses as well as standard dumbbells.

The weight of adjustable dumbbells depends on your fitness level and goals. Typically, they come in two main categories: those that max out at around 50 pounds per dumbbell and those that start at 50 pounds and get way heavier.

For beginners and folks looking to engage in moderate strength training at home, a set that maxes out at 50 pounds per dumbbell should suffice. They offer a range of weights for a wide variety of exercises and are a great starting point. Beginners can work on everything from biceps curls to overhead presses to squats with these.

Now, if you're a seasoned lifter, powerlifter, or someone aiming to build strength, opt for a pair of adjustable dumbbells that can go well above 50 pounds per bell. Adjustable sets from SMRTFT can offer a max of 80 pounds and 100 pounds per bell, respectively. For experienced lifters, added weight means greater versatility in tackling heavy exercises and challenging yourself.

Just like standard dumbbells, adjustable dumbbells are safe when used correctly and with proper form. But, as with any type of fitness equipment, there are some safety considerations to keep in mind.

It's important to choose adjustable dumbbells that are well-made and constructed from durable materials. If you're using an old-school model with removable plates, make sure they're securely attached to the handle before you start your lift.

The shape, feel, and weight distribution of adjustable dumbbells can take some getting used to, depending on the model you're working with. Because they may feel different compared to standard dumbbells in movements you do regularly, it's important to focus on slow, controlled movements and proper form throughout your workout (especially as you acclimate to them).

#4694. Energica rises from the ashes with plans for cheaper electric motorcycles

The Italian electric motorcycle maker, which ceased operations in 2024 after entering judicial liquidation, has announced a major revival under new international ownership. And while the Energica name is returning, the company behind it is going to look quite different this time around.

Perhaps the biggest change is where the motorcycles will actually be built.

Energica says motorcycle production is moving to Asia, while design, engineering, research and development, as well as responsibility for technical and quality standards, will remain in Italy. The new manufacturing setup is expected to significantly reduce production costs, allowing Energica to cut motorcycle prices by around 20% compared to its previous models.

That could be a big deal for a company whose motorcycles were widely praised for their performance and technology, but were also firmly positioned at the premium end of the market.

The revival comes after Energica was acquired by Energica Pte. Ltd., a Singapore-based company backed by international private investors. Importantly, much of the technological know-how isn’t disappearing overseas with the manufacturing. Energica says its core engineering and design leadership remains in Italy, including longtime CTO Giampiero Testoni and designer Paolo Imeni.

The first motorcycle to make its comeback will be the Energica Experia, the company’s adventure-oriented electric sport-tourer. After that, Energica plans to progressively restart production of the Ego, Eva Ribelle, and EsseEsse9, eventually bringing its entire previous lineup back to market.

At least initially, those motorcycles will use their existing platforms, which should help Energica get bikes rolling off the production line faster without having to develop and homologate entirely new machines. But upgrades are already planned, including a new battery and improvements to range, efficiency, performance, and reliability.

Energica is also specifically targeting Europe, the United States, and Australia as it rebuilds its dealer and service networks. Existing owners haven’t been forgotten either. The company says service has already resumed and spare-parts shipments have restarted to dealers in several countries.

For anyone who followed the electric motorcycle industry over the last decade, Energica’s disappearance was a particularly painful one. This wasn’t some startup with a couple of renderings and a dream. Energica built some of the highest-performance electric motorcycles on the road and spent four seasons supplying the motorcycles for the FIM MotoE World Cup, experience that helped develop its high-voltage and DC fast-charging technology.

Now the company gets something relatively rare in the motorcycle industry: a second chance.

And if moving production to Asia really can knock around 20% off Energica’s prices while retaining the Italian engineering that made the bikes special in the first place, Energica 2.0 might have a considerably better shot at turning great electric motorcycles into a sustainable business.

It seems like moving toward Asian manufacturing is all but inevitable here. It was the expensive European manufacturing of low-volume motorcycles that weighed so heavily on Energica’s balance sheets in the years up to their financial troubles, and so shifting production to countries with both the expertise and the cost benefits for motorcycle manufacturing simply makes sense.

Energica isn’t alone in discovering the economics of moving electric motorcycle production to Asia. Zero Motorcycles spent years manufacturing its bikes in California before beginning a major shift toward production in the Philippines in 2023, including both complete motorcycles and major subassemblies. Now the company works with multiple factories, including major manufacturers like Zongshen in China, to reduce production costs for its electric motorcycles while still maintaining the ‘designed in California’ marketing angle.

It’s too early to tell how the new strategy will play out for Energica, but the fact that the company is now following a more well-worn trail is a positive sign for those who have spent the last two years hoping for a revival.

#4693. Inside Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center, which doles out 10,000 pounds of food every day

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Cases of peanut butter, bright red boxes of Shredded Wheat cereal, and so many varieties of tea that even Mary Poppins would be excited. Around the corner, large wooden crates teeming with wide leaves and sturdy grasses, and a walk-in refrigerator full of fresh produce sit ready to turn into dishes that are a feast for the eyes and the belly.

For the team working at Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center (ANC) at Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida, it’s like Thanksgiving every day. The roughly 40 cast members on the animal nutrition team is responsible for feeding the over 5,000 animals at Disney’s Animal Kingdom Theme Park and The Seas at EPCOT. It takes time, a devotion to the science of nutrition, and really knowing your audience to deliver about 10,000 pounds of food per day. And like putting together any big meal, it requires a team effort, which extends well beyond the animals at Disney.

“What we’re trying to do is provide the optimal nutrition for animals to live long and healthy lives, and we do that by taking information from a lot of different fields,” Animal Nutrition Operations Manager Dr. Heidi Bissell tells Popular Science. “From the field of agriculture, we learn a lot about animal physiology and how animals work, and can then design diets with the ingredients we have for specific purposes.”

In addition to bringing in knowledge from across different scientific disciplines, the team collaborates with other accredited zoos, aquariums, and universities to share research and data on animal nutrition. They’ve published studies on animals from bigger animals like zebras and rhinos, to smaller fish and amphibians, which is crucial to filling in nutritional gaps. If the team is not sure what a particular species needs to eat in order to thrive, they will turn to comparative nutrition for answers.

“We go with a close relative [and] take what we know about the animals we do know a lot about and apply that to some of our other species,” Bissell explains. “Then we learn from our own animals by assessing how they’re doing on the diets that we’re offering, so we can gauge their nutritional status and make adjustments as needed.”

Staying nimble and making these adjustments is also important. If a supply chain issue disrupts what the nutrition team can get, having a back-up plan that includes nutritious food is critical. If an animal is familiar and comfortable with at least a few types of food, they will generally fare better, whether there are shortages or not.

At the same time, the nutrition team works to ensure that the food and its presentation mimics life in the wild as much as possible.

“Animals in the wild are spending their days solving puzzles, trying to figure out how to eat, while staying away from predators or toxins,” Bissell says. “They’re making a lot of decisions all day, so if we just offered them food in a bowl that would not provide them with mental stimulation.”

One of the most common behaviors is foraging, or digging through obstacles like grass, mud, or leaves to find food. The dishes the team creates are often presented in a way that encourages foraging, so that the animals keep up those natural behaviors. Leaves will be hung up in a tree for the giraffes to eat as they would in the wild. Carnivores like lions will get whole prey and bones to eat, which also helps keep their own jaws and teeth healthy. The team also pays attention to seasonal shifts to keep animals in their natural rhythm.

“Probably the biggest group of animals that we do this with would be birds,” says Bissell. “If they’re laying eggs, they might need more calcium, so we might add sources of calcium into their diet.”

Surprisingly, feeding bigger animals like lions and elephants is not as challenging as making sure that the insectivores have enough to eat. True to their name, anteaters almost exclusively eat bugs, and can consume up to 3,000 insects per day. To keep up with all of those the bugs, Bissell and the team work side-by-side with manufacturers to ensure their insect pellets meet the physical and nutritional standards needed to align with insects the anteaters encounter in the wild. To supplement, the anteaters will also get a bit of produce with the insects, since they do also eat fruit.

“We do a lot with like ice cakes, where we can freeze food in blocks of ice and can color the water with like vegetable dyes, so it’s fun and engaging. And the ice, especially in Florida in the summer, is really nice for hydration,” Bissell explains. “We are often pulling from what’s already in the animal diet or similar things, because just like humans, it’s not a great idea to just add a bunch of stuff on top of your existing diet.”

They’ll also follow themes, from a little fall pies to a driver’s license out of fruit and leaves for a gorilla’s 16th birthday and a food sculpture shaped like a margarita for a 21st birthday. That devotion to keeping meals fresh and creative helps all animals, humans included.

“I like making animals’ lives better, and by extension people’s lives better, because we care about these animals so much,” says Bissell.

#4691. What If Talking About Your Anxiety Isn't Helping?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

“What’s on your mind today?” “What’s been going on lately?” “What is activated for you today?” “How have you been feeling?"

Over the years, I have cycled through various go-to opening questions in my anxiety therapy sessions. Sometimes I don’t have to say a word: A client pulls open their Notes app or a journal the moment they sit down on the couch.

Yet, even if I ask the perfect question, or my client has already prepared a list of subjects for the session, the truth is: talking about anxiety doesn’t always lead to healing.

Anxiety runs in a loop. By the time the anxious client has entered my office, they have probably gone over these worries many times. Anxiety likes to replay the same line of thinking until it blurs the border between truth and fiction.

Anxiety venting encourages speaking in extremes, which sometimes distorts our thinking. The other person in the conversation may feel the need to validate our emotions and be supportive, but our brains can interpret this social nicety as an agreement with the content of our worries.

When we engage in a monologue about our anxiety, we are effectively overthinking out loud.

Our brain is trying to self-soothe by overthinking. The hope is that thinking will lead to a solution, clarity, or insight, and then we will feel much better. But as we all know, overthinking our worries can be counterproductive at best and dysregulating at worst.

Thinking about and talking about worries can deepen anxiety. When we spiral down into our thoughts, we go deeper into our heads. We can get lost in the effort to figure out our thoughts.

As an anxiety therapist, my job is to break the cycle of overthinking and help my client spiral up into action. Sometimes, this means that we cannot spend our session talking about anxiety. We cannot analyze and replay the anxious line of thinking.

The remedy for overthinking is an action that takes you out of your head and back into your life. We change our behavior to change our mindset.

For certain people, such action takes the form of ERP (exposure response prevention). In this type of therapy, a person intentionally faces fears and resists compulsions (including overthinking).

Exposure therapy is quite different from traditional talk therapy. In this approach, a person creates and executes a brave to-do list (formally known as an exposure hierarchy). For example, a person worried about speaking up to their boss practices role-playing the conversation and then sends an email to get a meeting on the books. Someone anxious about driving at night practices driving two blocks in their neighborhood at dusk. The aim is to create a pathway toward facing fears rather than thinking and talking about them.

Exposure therapy means committing to action rather than staying stuck in the analysis of anxiety.

This is not to say that talking about one’s anxiety is never helpful. In some cases, the other person in an anxiety conversation is a valuable source of insight.

When anxiety has caused someone to depart significantly from reality, sharing one’s worries can be grounding. The second person might be able to show where the worrier has created anxious distortions—self-blaming, catastrophizing, or personalizing.

Talking about one’s anxiety also helps when someone feels very alone in their worries. Having a person to share with can help the worrier feel supported, even if the other cannot change their mindset.

Conversations about anxiety will happen, inside and outside of the therapy room. Following these guidelines can help make sure the talk is productive.

Anxious looping is all about repeating the same well-worn thoughts without making progress. Notice and stop yourself if you are doing this out loud. You are perpetuating a cycle.

Too often, we seek insight from another person, but then ignore their view. If you are deep in your anxious worry, someone else’s thoughts are likely a helpful anchor to reality. Do not immediately dismiss what you are hearing from your trusted confidante.

Discussing your anxiety can be productive to a point, but notice if it is interfering with taking real action. Anxiety can be paralyzing. Remember that spiraling up often involves taking one brave step toward a fear.

Be aware of how discussing your anxiety is taking you out of your present moment. Are you less connected to today because you are talking about fears for the future or worries about the past? Conversations can help people cope, but sometimes they pull people deeper into thought.

If you are stuck, take a break from talking about worries. Instead, today, do one small thing for yourself that brings joy.

#4690. Tesla to end Cybertruck production as sales stall at ~10% of plan

Tesla is ending Cybertruck production. CEO Elon Musk announced early Friday that the automaker will “wind down” the electric pickup at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of 2027, about three and a half years after the first deliveries.

Musk says it’s to make room for more Cybercab production. But Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck is short on buyers, and it sells at roughly a tenth of the 250,000 units a year Tesla built its line for.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

That’s all he said. Nothing yet on how long Tesla will keep selling inventory or what happens to parts and service for existing owners.

Tesla doesn’t break out Cybertruck deliveries. It lumps them into “Other Models,” along with the Model S, Model X, and now the Semi.

That bucket tells the story anyway. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3 2026, down 48% year-over-year and the lowest since Q2 2021. With Model S and Model X production over since April, we estimated that 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks.

That’s a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. Tesla planned the Cybertruck line for 250,000 units annually, and its latest shareholder letter still lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. So the truck is selling at about 12% of plan, and roughly a quarter of what’s actually installed.

The US numbers from Cox Automotive are worse. Cox estimates 3,519 Cybertruck sales in Q1 2026 and 3,744 in Q2, down from 14,416 in Q3 2024.

And not all of those were real customers. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, and Musk’s companies took 1,339 in total, about 19% of US registrations that quarter. If it wasn’t for Musk’s self-dealing, the Cybertruck would probably be dead already.

Tesla tried to fix demand. It launched a cheaper rear-wheel-drive version in 2025 and pulled it months later, then brought a cheaper dual-motor trim to customers this summer. And then it raised prices by $5,000 in August. The dual-motor now starts at $74,990.

The “make room” explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of factory floor, by Tesla’s own count, and the Cybertruck line is already running at about a quarter of its installed capacity. Most of it is sitting idle.

The Cybercab also isn’t at a volume where it’s fighting anyone for floor space. Texas had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October, and Tesla built a separate line for its “unboxed” manufacturing process.

If Tesla needs more Cybercab capacity down the road, it has the space. What it doesn’t want is to keep paying for a truck with its own stainless steel body, its own castings, and its own supply chain at 30,000 units a year.

Let’s call this what it is. Tesla isn’t ending the Cybertruck because the Cybercab needs room. It’s ending it because nobody’s buying it at anything close to the volume Tesla planned, and supporting a low-volume vehicle this unique is expensive.

I wouldn’t be surprised if Tesla lost a couple of billions on the Cybertruck experiment. Between R&D, pushing suppliers to produce 250,000 trucks per year, and deploying its own production line capable of 125,000 trucks per year, Tesla has invested billions. And with only ~70,000 trucks delivered in roughly 3 years, it probably never made any positive cash flow from the program.

They are just in-between growth phases. No need to panic just because they have discontinued three vehicles and the last successful vehicle they launched was the Model Y in early 2020.

The Cybercab line gives Musk a forward-looking reason to wrap a product failure in. Tesla did the same thing when it ended Model S and Model X production this year to free up Fremont for Optimus. It’s a lot easier to say “we need room for the future” than “this didn’t sell.”

We’ve said it many times: the Cybertruck is genuinely impressive to drive. Steer-by-wire and rear-wheel steering are real engineering, and nobody else has put them in a production pickup. But Tesla built a 250,000-unit factory for a polarizing $75,000+ truck that can’t be sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets. It just cancelled it for Australia and New Zealand two weeks ago. The math was never going to work.

It’s truly a sign of Tesla today. Musk used to talk about having a more traditional electric truck design if Cybertruck fails, but I doubt we will see that. Again, Elon is betting the house on autonomy.

#4689. NASA teases experimental X-70 ‘Fractal’ aircraft

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:00 AM EST

NASA has unveiled its next experimental aircraft, dubbed the X-70 Fractal. Well, “unveiled” may be a bit of a stretch. During this week’s UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman announced plans for the “crewed, high-performance platform” designed to boost maneuverability, flight control, and “other cutting-edge technologies in real flight.”

Beyond that, you’re guess is probably about as good as anyone’s. Even X-70’s sole visual hint may mean nothing at all. The shadowy frame seen silhouetted by fog in NASA’s announcement is explicitly identified as AI “generated content.” This means even the rounded cockpit, splayed tail fins, and extended wings may ultimately not even show up in the final design.

Despite a lack of photographs, NASA did provide some more concrete details about the X-70. The aircraft will have a 10,000 pound takeoff weight and will cruise at Mach .75 (about 570 miles per hour) at a maximum altitude of 45,000 feet. Its operational range is also expected to exceed 1,500 nautical miles (1,726 miles).

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” NASA Research and Technology Mission Directorate director Laurie Grindle said in the agency’s announcement. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

NASA also emphasized the X-70’s modular construction, which will allow quick swaps of internal and external payloads. As The War Zone noted, these features are likely intended to facilitate tests of experimental autonomous deployments and drone technology. The X-70 may also feature “bleeding-edge” abilities like morphing wings and “air-burst” controls, which allow aircraft to precisely maneuver midflight solely through blasts of pressurized air.

Isaacman said he expects the X-70 to complete its first flight within the next two years, although it’s always useful to take experimental aircraft timelines with a grain of salt. When NASA awarded Lockheed Martin the contract to develop its X-59 aircraft in 2016, the aim was to have a vehicle ready for testing by 2020. The actual X-59’s maiden flight ultimately took place on October 28, 2025.

#4687. The 7 Best Wired Headphones for Your Runs and Workouts

No more charging, no more lost Bluetooth connections, and no more chasing a bud under the squat rack.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WIRED HEADPHONES ARE popular again. The cords are showing up in NBA arena tunnels, where Golden State Warriors point guard Steph Curry walks in with them hanging from his ears. Bears quarterback Caleb Williams wears corded headphones as part of his pregame routine. Bose felt they were worth bringing back, too. In October, it started shipping the $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds, its first new wired headphones in years.While our favorite wireless workout headphones are more advanced than ever, they still have problems at the gym: connections drop, audio crackles, and you have to constantly manage the battery. And we've all had a bud knocked loose by a burpee and watched it bounce across the floor and under a squat rack. Just me? A wired pair avoids all of that. Sound travels through the cable, so there are no Bluetooth dropouts, and if a bud slips out, it hangs from the cord instead of hitting the ground.

Wired earbuds also have no battery. You'll never get to the gym and find out your headphones are dead, and a pair that's been sitting in your bag for a month still works as soon as you plug it in.

Sure, the cord can have its own drawbacks. It can snag on a rack in the gym, and when you run, it can bounce around into your body and arms. Its weight also pulls the buds downward, which can put pressure on your ears.

Most picks below have a way to keep the buds in place, including ear hooks, stabilizer wings, or a cable that runs over the top of your ear. Most also come with the right plug for your phone, so you don’t need an adapter. These are the best wired headphones you can get right now.

The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are the only pair on this list with active noise canceling. Each bud has two microphones that pick up the clang of plates and the music on the gym speakers, then cancel that sound. With the room quieter, you can keep your own music at a lower volume. Hold the button on the inline remote to switch to Aware mode. It uses the same mics to pipe in outside sound, so you can hear cars and cyclists on an outdoor run.

Noise canceling works best when each bud seals your ear canal, and silicone wing-tip stabilizers keep that seal in place while you move. Bose’s wings press against the inner ridge of your ear, so the buds don't shift during jumps or sprints. You get two wing sizes and three ear tip sizes, and you can remove the wings if you don't need them. The thick, rubbery 4.2-foot cable connecting them is durable. It tangles less than the thin cords on cheap USB-C buds, and it makes less noise when it rubs against a shirt.

Partway down that cable sits the remote, which holds volume buttons, a multifunction button (tap to play or pause, double-tap to skip, hold to change noise modes), and the call mic. All that hardware can be heavy, though — enough that you'll feel it pull on the buds during jumps and sprints. Running the cable under your shirt collar keeps the remote from swinging.

The noise canceling also determines what you can plug these into. The earbuds draw power from your phone to run the mics and processor, so they need a USB-C port. Any iPhone 15 or newer works, and most current Android phones do too. A 3.5mm jack, like the one on a treadmill screen or an airplane seat, won't work, even with an adapter. Once they're plugged in, the IPX4 rating protects them from sweat and splashes from any direction, though not from a dunk in water. They come in black, white, and a limited-edition mint.

Read more: Best Workout Headphones, Tested by Us

The JBL Endurance Run 3 costs $25 and carries an IP65 rating, the highest on this list. That means no dust gets in on dirt trails and sandy beach runs, while they can survive water sprayed from a nozzle. A downpour or a sweat-soaked HIIT class won't hurt them, either.

JBL's FlipHook design gives you two ways to wear them. With the cable hanging straight down, they sit like regular earbuds. Rotate the hooks upward and the cable runs over the top of your ear and down behind it. That takes the cable's weight off the bud. It also stops the wire from thumping against your chest while you run and jump. The TwistLock tips sit into the bowl of your ear, so a bud stays put when you turn your head fast.

The remote has one button and a mic, handling play, pause, and calls, and a long press brings up Siri or Google Assistant. You can adjust the volume through your phone. The standard Run 3 plugs into a 3.5mm jack. JBL also offers the Endurance Run 3C USB-C, which has a three-button remote and costs a little more. The standard Endurance Run 3 has a 3.5mm plug and a one-button remote.

The MEE Audio M6 Sport uses memory wire, a thin, bendable wire inside the cable near each bud. You bend it around the back of your ear once, and it holds that curve. It works like a custom-fit ear hook that stays put through box jumps and hill sprints, and it also takes stress off the buds.

The three-button remote on the braided cable does more than most wired sport buds. The outer buttons raise and lower volume. The center button plays, pauses, skips tracks, answers calls, and starts your voice assistant. The IPX5 rating protects against heavy sweat and rain.

MEE Audio tunes the M6 Sport for heavy bass. The USB-C version works with modern smartphones, and it comes with a shirt clip and six sets of ear tips, so you can get the exact fit you want. You can also get them a with a 3.5mm jack plug..

The SE215 earphones are in-ear monitors, the same style of earphones musicians wear on stage to hear themselves over a loud crowd. The low-profile shells sit flush inside your ear. The cable runs up and over the back of each ear, pulling the cord's weight off the buds and keeping cable noise out of your music when you move. The included foam tips expand to fill your ear canal, and Shure says they block up to 37 decibels of outside noise, enough to drown out a gym's speakers.

The SE215 delivers deeper bass than other wired headphones we’ve tested. Beyond sound, the earbuds have also been designed with durability in mind. The SE215's cable is Kevlar-reinforced and detaches at MMCX connectors, so if it breaks, you only replace the cord. Shure also sells a Bluetooth adapter that makes the same buds wireless.

Shure doesn't give them an IP rating, though, so you should wipe them down after sweaty sessions. The standard 64-inch cable has no mic or remote and comes only in a 3.5mm configuration, so a USB-C phone needs a dongle.

Apple’s EarPods are the pair you see a lot of people using in TikTok videos, holding the mic close to their mouth. At $19, they’re a great pair to keep in your bag for the day you forget your main headphones. The remote has volume buttons and a center button to play, pause, and answer calls. Apple says they're protected against sweat and water, though it doesn't list an IP rating.

The EarPods have hard plastic shells shaped to rest in the bowl of your ear, with no silicone tips sealing the canal. That makes them comfortable for long walks and lets outside sound in. But nothing holds them in place for more rigorous movements like burpees and jump rope. Still, they're steady enough for walking, the elliptical, and light lifting.

Read more: Our Review of the Apple iPhone Duo

The Avantree C171’s ear hooks are molded to curve over and behind each ear, so unlike the MEE Audio M6 Sport, no wire needs to be bent into shape. The cable runs down behind your ear instead of hanging from the bud, so it’s more out of the way when you’re moving.

A four-button remote controls volume, playback, calls, and your voice assistant, so you can keep your phone in your pocket. Avantree sells similar sport earbuds with USB-C, Lightning, and 3.5mm plugs; the C171 is the USB-C model, and the brand’s C171 manual includes troubleshooting for Galaxy S24 users who run into audio detection or distortion issues.

They don’t have an IP rating, but if fit is your main concern, these shouldn’t fly out of your ear during a HIIT workout.

The Avantree Resolve's speakers rest just outside your ear canal instead of sealing inside it, so you can still hear traffic and cyclists coming up behind you on a run. With no tip pressing into your ear canal, you'll also feel less soreness that builds up over a long session.

Since nothing sits inside your ear to hold the speakers in place, flexible hooks wrap over each ear to hold them in place. That grip won't be as snug as an in-ear tip, so the speakers can shift more when you move. Avantree makes a Small-Medium size for ears under 2.5 inches long and a Large size for everyone else, so measure your ear before you order.

While there is no IP rating, you do get inline remote controls for playback, volume, calls, and your voice assistant. Avantree sells 3.5mm, USB-C, and Lightning versions.

Wired headphones are better if your workouts keep getting cut short by dead batteries or bad Bluetooth connections. Without a battery, wired headphones play as soon as you plug them in, no matter how long they've sat unused. There's also no battery to wear out after two or three years of charging, which is when many wireless earbuds start dying mid-run.

Wireless buds are the better choice when you need total freedom of movement. Rolling on the floor, kipping pull-ups, and jump rope can all snag a cord. If your workouts are mostly lifting, steady running, or cardio machines, a cord rarely gets in the way.

Like any earbud, whether it’s wired or wireless, they can fall out of your ear. The cable's weight pulls on each bud with every step, so look for one of three fixes: ear hooks, like the memory wire on the MEE Audio M6 Sport or the FlipHook on the JBL Endurance Run 3, loop the cable over your ear. Stability wings, like those on the Bose, brace the bud against the ridge inside your ear. Over-ear cable routing, as on the Shure SE215, takes the cable's weight off the bud entirely. Plain earbuds with no tips or wings, like Apple's EarPods, are the most likely to fall out.

Yes, if you match the plug to your phone. USB-C earbuds plug straight into an iPhone 15 and later and most Android phones. Their digital-to-analog converter is built into the plug or cable, so you don't need an adapter. Since most modern smartphones no longer have a 3.5mm jack, earbuds with a 3.5mm plug need a USB-C-to-3.5mm dongle, and on a run that dongle adds weight and can snag on equipment. Choose a USB-C version when one exists.

The thumping you hear when the cord bounces against your shirt is called microphonic. Vibration travels up the wire into the earbud. Routing the cable over your ears is the most effective fix because it breaks the straight path from your chest to your ear canal. Running the cable under your shirt collar also stops it from swinging. A thicker, rubberized cable, like Bose's, transmits less noise than a thin plastic one.

IPX4 is the minimum for sweaty workouts. An IP rating has two digits. The first is dust protection on a scale up to 6, and the second is water protection on a scale up to 9. An X means the product wasn't tested for that category. IPX4 protects against splashing water from any direction, which covers sweat. An IPX5 rating means the headphones can withstand water jets, but it doesn’t guarantee protection in every condition, such as heavy rain. IP65, the JBL Endurance Run 3's rating, adds full dust protection for trail running.

Water and dust resistance is one area where wireless earbuds are well ahead. Most wireless workout models are rated at least IPX4, and many are rated IP55 or higher. Only three of the wired picks here have a rating: the Bose, the JBL, and the MEE Audio. If your pair doesn't have one, they can still survive light sweat, but remember to wipe them dry after each session.

I use Apple’s EarPods every day and have spent years testing wireless headphones and earbuds. That experience shaped what I looked for here. For this guide, I picked models based on factors like fit, durability, compatibility, and inline controls. The rest of the Men's Health team also reviewed and contributed to the list.

First, I looked at fit. A cable pulls on the buds every time you move, so I looked for ear hooks, stabilizer wings, or cables that run over the ear. I favored pairs with an official IP rating over vague "sweat-resistant" claims. I also checked that each pair is sold with a plug that fits current phones, because a 3.5mm-to-USB-C adapter is one more thing that can come loose mid-run. Inline controls mattered as well, since a remote you can reach mid-set means you don't have to dig your phone out.

#4686. Baby whale surprises scientists

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:33 AM EST

The 2027 North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) baby season has officially begun. The calving season lasts from November through April, and is a particularly important stretch of time given that the species is classified as critically endangered by the IUCN Red List.

Due to their low numbers, scientists are closely monitoring these baleen whales. Yet even with all of that surveillance, one whale managed to keep a secret up until September.Experts spotted a known female and her previously unidentified calf from last calving season near Anticosti Island, Quebec, Canada, according to the New England Aquarium.

The 38-year-old female right whale is called Silt. In addition to being a mother, Silt is  also a grandmother and great-grandmother. The new calf is her sixth baby known to scientists.

“Silt managed to fly under the radar of survey teams throughout the spring and summer,” according to the aquarium “Although we don’t know exactly when or where her calf was born, she was briefly seen in the southeastern United States calving grounds in February, so it’s possible the calf was born there.”

More North Atlantic right whales are always good news. They are one of the most endangered large whales, and are vulnerable to ship collisions and fishing gear entanglement. Almost exactly a year ago, we were happy to report that the species is showing signs of slowly rebounding. 2024’s estimate of around 384 North Atlantic right whales represents a 2.1 percent increase from 2023’s estimate.

“The population increase is really good news, and so far, what we’ve seen in 2025 is also good news,” New England Aquarium senior scientist Heather Pettis told Popular Science in October 2025 . But “we’re talking about a population of 384 individual whales—that’s still incredibly low,” she added. “Yes, we’re seeing increases. They’re small, and we still are seeing injuries to animals from human activities. And so, you know, I say that we’re cautiously optimistic.”

#4685. BYD’s electric hypercar hits 312 mph, first production car over 500 km/h

BYD’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme just reached 503.17 km/h (312.66 mph) on a closed highway in Abu Dhabi, making it the first production car ever to go faster than 500 km/h.

The FIA and Guinness World Records both recognized the run. It’s the all-electric hypercar’s second top-speed record in just over a year, and the one it broke was its own.

BYD announced the record on X this morning, saying the U9 Xtreme “has done the impossible” and calling it “the fastest production car on the planet.”

Abu Dhabi closed a 10 km section of the Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road (E11), in the emirate’s Al Dhafra Region, for the attempt. That gave the team a 7 km straight. Marc Basseng, the German racing driver who set the car’s previous record, was behind the wheel again.

It took two days. Basseng maxed out at 490 km/h on the first day, per the FIA. After an overnight round of changes to the rear wing, damping, and tire pressures, he got to 503.17 km/h on his second attempt of November 1.

The previous mark was 496.22 km/h (308 mph), set at Germany’s ATP Papenburg proving ground in September 2025. That run had already pushed the Bugatti Chiron Super Sport 300+ and its 490.48 km/h from 2019 off the top of the list.

And it comes just days after BYD released footage of a U9 Xtreme crashing into a guardrail at about 280 mph during an earlier high-speed test. The driver walked away unharmed. BYD went right back out and hit 457.89 km/h on the next run.

The U9 Xtreme is the track-focused version of the Yangwang U9, the flagship supercar from BYD’s luxury brand. It uses four electric motors, each rated at 555 kW and spinning up to 30,000 rpm, for 2,220 kW combined. That’s over 3,000 PS, or nearly 3,000 hp.

It runs on a 1,200-volt architecture with a track-grade version of BYD’s Blade Battery. Those are LFP cells, the same chemistry BYD puts in its cheapest city cars.

For context, the Rimac Nevera R, which snagged a pile of EV world records last year, tops out at 431.45 km/h. The U9 Xtreme also holds the production EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife at 6:59.157.

Only 30 will be built, and BYD is charging around $3 million apiece. Don’t expect to see one in the US, where BYD doesn’t sell passenger cars.

The biggest one: this is a single-direction run. The two Guinness titles listed for the attempt, highest speed by a production car and by an electric production car, are both specified as “single direction.” BYD’s post claims four Guinness records, but the FIA’s announcement only lists those two for this run.

Production car top speed records have traditionally been the average of two runs in opposite directions, within an hour, to cancel out wind and road grade. That’s how Koenigsegg got its 447.19 km/h record with the Agera RS in 2017.

Bugatti took heat for exactly this in 2019, when the Chiron hit 490 km/h one way on a pre-production car. Bugatti itself said it wasn’t an official record.

The car also ran on bespoke semi-slick tires developed with Giti Tire. It’s not clear whether the 30 customer cars will get them.

A Chinese automaker best known for $10,000 city cars now builds the fastest production car in the world, and it’s electric. Not long ago, the conventional wisdom was that EVs couldn’t sustain high top speeds because the battery and motors would overheat long before the car ran out of road. BYD just ran 503 km/h on LFP cells. LFP cells!

But we’d hold BYD to the same standard we held Bugatti to. A one-way run on a highway with a 7 km straight is a great demo, not a definitive record, but impressive nonetheless.

Roadster 2 will now never be a record holder. It simple can't compete with today's hypercars nevermind those in 2028 when we actually see one leave a factory. Although with Tesla's record, it's usually 4 years from demo to production so that makes it 2030 for the Roadster 2.

And either way, let’s be honest: this is about marketing. Nobody is going to drive one of these 30 cars at 500 km/h. But it works. It’s a halo for Yangwang ahead of its new ultra-luxury sedan and for BYD’s push into Europe, and it makes the “Chinese cars are cheap copies” crowd look out of date.

Meanwhile, Tesla promised a Roadster that would hit over 250 mph back in 2017. Nine years later, it’s still not in production.

The real question now is whether Bugatti or Koenigsegg answers with a two-way 500 km/h run. Koenigsegg says its Jesko Absolut can theoretically do it, but it has never attempted a run. Is BYD what finally makes them try?

#4684. Why a Short Week Can Feel So Long

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

In interviews for my research on leaders, I asked executives to describe a difficult week. One leader talked me through an annual report, tax paperwork, fundraising, board work, and decisions about products and events. When I asked what was hard, she didn't single out any one task, but said, “It's not that those things are too much; it's just the changing of direction every day.”

She could handle the questions, meetings, and requests. What wore her down was having to stop all the normal stuff to deal with the annual report or tax filing, then switch to something else, and then figure out where she'd left off.

I drive my ninth-grade son to school, and yesterday he said it “felt like a long school week.” Interestingly, he had Tuesday off, an early dismissal Wednesday, and a late start Thursday… he actually spent less time at school. So, how could it feel longer!?

It reminded me of the leader story. He and I talked about routines and how little attention we pay to things when we know what comes next. Bottom line… it felt exhausting to have his normal schedule interrupted.

Let's go take a look at what research says about having to change directions so often.

What did our interrupted leader do? She tried to put some order around the week, setting aside one morning for product development and another stretch of time for board work. Then an event would need attention, or another responsibility would intrude. One day, a staff member left with little notice, and the website, online store, and event preparation were back on her desk. She could plan the week, but keeping it that way was basically impossible.

In 2001, researchers Joshua Rubinstein and his colleagues asked people to switch back and forth between simple tasks, like sorting shapes or doing math. Even small changes took extra time. Harder tasks made it worse, while a clue about what was coming next helped. This wasn't the same as someone interrupting you at work, but it shows that changing gears isn't free. My son knew that his strange school schedule would be back to normal the following week, but the executive had no idea what would interrupt her next.

But the lost time isn't the only issue. I get to interview spouses in my work. The leader mentioned above? Her husband saw what those days did to her. He told me she came home worn out with a long to-do list still on her mind. When she couldn't finish it, he said it “really puts a burden... a strain, on her.” Researcher Sophie Leroy studied something similar in 2009. In two experiments, she found that people had trouble letting go of a task they hadn't finished. Even after moving on to something else, part of their attention was still on the earlier job. She called that “attention residue.”

Think about sitting down to talk with an employee while you're still worrying about the budget you left unfinished.

Here's the most surprising finding to me around this subject: in 2008, Gloria Mark and her colleagues had people do typical office email tasks. Some were interrupted by calls or instant messages. The interrupted people actually finished their work FASTER… and their work wasn't noticeably worse (although their email replies were shorter). So why not be interrupted all day if you’re more productive? Those interrupted workers felt more stressed, frustrated, and rushed, and said the work took more effort.

The executive's week wasn't hard because of any one task. It was having to stop, switch, and figure out where she'd left off, over and over again. My son's week wasn't harder because of the assignments. It was having to think about what comes next and what comes after and hold that in the front of his mind.

Remember Sophie Leroy's finding about “attention residue”? In 2018, she and Theresa Glomb tested a way to reduce it. In their studies, people took a moment before switching tasks to think about where they'd stopped and how they'd pick up again. They called it a “ready-to-resume” plan. It helped people focus on the new task instead of worrying so much about the unfinished one.

So, here's how to fix a heavy, mixed-up week. You're halfway through a report when the phone rings. Before taking the call, jot down where you stopped and what you'll do next when you return. That's it. Now you can give the caller your attention without trying to remember every detail of the unfinished report.

My son's schedule will be back to normal next week. The executive can't count on that. But when she has to change direction, she can take a moment to write down where she left off. That won't stop the interruptions, but it will keep her from spending so much time trying to get back to work.

To lead sustainably, when you have to stop what you're doing, take a moment to plan how you'll start again.

Leroy, S. (2009). Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 109(2), 168–181. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2009.04.002

Leroy, S., & Glomb, T. M. (2018). Tasks interrupted: How anticipating time pressure on resumption of an interrupted task causes attention residue and low performance on interrupting tasks and how a “ready-to-resume” plan mitigates the effects. Organization Science, 29(3), 380–397. https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2017.1184

Mark, G., Gudith, D., & Klocke, U. (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 107–110. https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072

Rubinstein, J. S., Meyer, D. E., & Evans, J. E. (2001). Executive control of cognitive processes in task switching. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 27(4), 763–797. https://doi.org/10.1037/0096-1523.27.4.763
